fact: SUSE Rancher Prime is installed from the rancher-prime Helm chart repository, added with `helm repo add rancher-prime <helm-chart-repo-url>`. The repository URL is published in the Prime-only documentation, which requires logging in with SUSE Customer Center (SCC) credentials.
The Rancher chart must be installed into the `cattle-system` namespace, created with `kubectl create namespace cattle-system`. The Helm release name in that namespace should always be `rancher`.

With the default Rancher-generated certificates, SUSE Rancher Prime is installed with `helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system --set hostname=rancher.my.org --set bootstrapPassword=admin`, replacing the hostname with your DNS name and setting a unique bootstrap password. `ingress.tls.source` is not specified because `rancher` is its default.
command: helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system --set hostname=rancher.my.org --set bootstrapPassword=admin

fact: The Rancher chart option `ingress.tls.source` selects the certificate source: `rancher` (Rancher-generated, the default), `letsEncrypt`, or `secret` (certificates from files). cert-manager is required for `rancher` and `letsEncrypt`, but not for `secret`.

After installing or upgrading Rancher with Helm, check that it rolled out with `kubectl -n cattle-system rollout status deploy/rancher`. If it reports that the deployment exceeded its progress deadline, run `kubectl -n cattle-system get deploy rancher` and compare DESIRED with AVAILABLE.

If no bootstrap password was set at install time, Rancher generates one. It can be retrieved with `kubectl get secret --namespace cattle-system bootstrap-secret -o go-template='{{ .data.bootstrapPassword|base64decode}}{{ "\n" }}'`.
command: kubectl get secret --namespace cattle-system bootstrap-secret -o go-template='{{ .data.bootstrapPassword|base64decode}}{{ "\n" }}'

fact: To reset the administrator password on a Helm (Kubernetes) install, exec `reset-password` in a Rancher pod: `kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password`.
command: kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password

fact: If the last admin was deleted or deactivated on a Helm install, run `ensure-default-admin` in a Rancher pod: `kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher | grep '1/1' | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -- ensure-default-admin`.
command: kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher | grep '1/1' | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -- ensure-default-admin

fact: The only tested and supported upgrade path between Rancher minor versions is from the latest patch of your current minor release to the latest patch of the next minor release (for example v2.13.x to v2.14.x). If you are not on the latest patch, upgrade to it first.
To see which Rancher Prime chart versions are available, run `helm repo update` and then `helm search repo rancher-prime/rancher --versions`.

Before a Rancher upgrade, capture the values used at install with `helm get values rancher -n cattle-system`. To reuse them, export them to a file with `helm get values rancher -n cattle-system -o yaml > values.yaml`.
command: helm get values rancher -n cattle-system -o yaml > values.yaml

fact: To upgrade Rancher Prime while keeping existing settings and changing only the version, run `helm upgrade rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system -f values.yaml --version={current-patch-version}` using the values exported from the current release.
command: helm upgrade rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system -f values.yaml --version={current-patch-version}

fact: Before upgrading Rancher, back up the Rancher server with the Rancher Backups application to use as a restore point. Also review installed Rancher feature charts (Apps > Installed Apps) and upgrade them to the latest version within their current chart release line.

Rolling Rancher back to a previous version is only possible by restoring a backup made before the upgrade with the Rancher Backups application; changing versions using kubectl or Helm is not supported. Rolling back to an end-of-life version is not supported.

After restoring the pre-upgrade backup, Rancher is rolled back to the previous version with `helm rollback rancher -n cattle-system`; use `helm history rancher -n cattle-system` to pick a specific revision.

The rancher-backup operator (Rancher Backups app) is installed only on the local cluster that runs the Rancher server and backs up only the Rancher application. It is installed from Cluster Management > local > Explore > Apps > Charts > Rancher Backups, and only Rancher admins and the local cluster's cluster-owner can use it.

The rancher-backup operator adds three cluster-scoped CRDs: backups.resources.cattle.io, restores.resources.cattle.io and resourcesets.resources.cattle.io. A Backup custom resource produces a .tar.gz file in the configured storage location, and a Restore custom resource restores from such a file.

Two ResourceSets are maintained for Rancher: rancher-resource-set-full (includes essential secrets) and rancher-resource-set-basic (no secrets). Use rancher-resource-set-full in production; since public API tokens are backed by secrets (Rancher 2.13+), basic is no longer suitable for production.

To encrypt backups, store the EncryptionConfiguration in a secret in cattle-resources-system whose key is encryption-provider-config.yaml: `kubectl create secret generic encryptionconfig --from-file=./encryption-provider-config.yaml -n cattle-resources-system`, then reference it with encryptionConfigSecretName. The operator does not save the EncryptionConfiguration file, so you must keep it for restores.
command: kubectl create secret generic encryptionconfig --from-file=./encryption-provider-config.yaml -n cattle-resources-system

fact: S3 credentials for rancher-backup are a secret with keys accessKey and secretKey, created with `kubectl create secret generic s3-creds --from-literal=accessKey=<access key> --from-literal=secretKey=<secret key>` and referenced via credentialSecretName/credentialSecretNamespace. It can live in any namespace and is unnecessary if EC2 nodes have IAM permissions for the bucket.
command: kubectl create secret generic s3-creds --from-literal=accessKey=<access key> --from-literal=secretKey=<secret key>

fact: Only one default storage location can be configured at the rancher-backup operator level: an S3-compatible object store, an existing StorageClass, an existing persistent volume, or none. Individual backups can override it only with an S3-compatible store. PVs used for backups should use the Retain reclaim policy.
Restore progress is followed in the rancher-backup operator logs: `kubectl logs -n cattle-resources-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rancher-backup -f`.

During an in-place restore the operator scales down the Rancher deployment and scales it back up when the restore completes, so Rancher is unavailable during the restore. Resources are restored in the order: CRDs, then cluster-scoped resources, then namespaced resources.

A Restore custom resource names the backup file with backupFilename. Encrypted backups have a .enc suffix and need encryptionConfigSecretName pointing to a secret with the same contents used at backup time. prune (enabled by default and recommended) deletes Rancher-managed resources not present in the backup.

When migrating Rancher to a new cluster with rancher-backup, do not install Rancher on the new cluster first, set prune: false in the Restore, and use the same hostname as the original server URL; otherwise downstream clusters show as unavailable.

On a new cluster, the rancher-backup charts come from the rancher-charts repository, added with `helm repo add rancher-charts https://charts.rancher.io`, and are installed as rancher-backup-crd and then rancher-backup in cattle-resources-system.

The rancher-backup CRD chart is installed first with `helm install rancher-backup-crd rancher-charts/rancher-backup-crd -n cattle-resources-system --create-namespace --version $CHART_VERSION`, followed by `helm install rancher-backup rancher-charts/rancher-backup -n cattle-resources-system --version $CHART_VERSION`, where CHART_VERSION is compatible with your Rancher version.
After applying a Restore during migration, watch it with `kubectl get restore`; once the Restore status is Completed, continue with installing cert-manager and Rancher.

When migrating Rancher between different Kubernetes distributions (for example K3s to RKE2), after the restore and before starting Rancher, edit the local cluster object with `kubectl edit clusters.management.cattle.io local`: set status.driver to imported, remove status.provider, status.version, the provider.cattle.io label, the management.cattle.io/current-cluster-controllers-version annotation, and spec.rke2Config or spec.k3sConfig.

After migrating and redirecting traffic, scale the original Rancher instance to zero so it stops contacting managed clusters: `kubectl scale deployment rancher -n cattle-system --replicas=0`. Leaving it up can leave clusters stuck in Updating in the new environment.

If downstream clusters do not reconnect to a migrated Rancher after traffic is redirected, restart the agent on each downstream cluster with `kubectl rollout restart deployment cattle-cluster-agent -n cattle-system`.
command: kubectl rollout restart deployment cattle-cluster-agent -n cattle-system

fact: Existing clusters are registered (imported) via ☰ > Cluster Management > Import Existing, choosing the cluster type, then running the generated kubectl command on a machine whose kubeconfig points at the cluster. With self-signed Rancher certificates, use the displayed curl command instead to avoid 'certificate signed by unknown authority'.

Registering a cluster requires cluster-admin privileges in it; grant them with `kubectl create clusterrolebinding cluster-admin-binding --clusterrole cluster-admin --user [USER_ACCOUNT]`. This is needed on GKE because cluster-admin is not granted by default.

A newly registered cluster is in Pending state while Rancher deploys its resources and becomes accessible once Active. Active clusters get two projects: Default (namespace default) and System (cattle-system, kube-public, kube-system and others if present). A cluster that is currently active in a Rancher setup cannot be re-registered.

Deleting a registered cluster from Rancher only detaches it: the cluster keeps running and is accessible as before registration. By contrast, an EKS, AKS or GKE cluster created by Rancher is destroyed when deleted in Rancher.

If a registered cluster stays Pending with 'Waiting for full cluster configuration', the cattle-cluster-agent cannot connect to the configured server-url. Check the agent pod with `kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=cattle-cluster-agent -o wide`.
command: kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=cattle-cluster-agent -o wide

fact: Logs of the cluster agent on a registered cluster are read with `kubectl -n cattle-system logs -l app=cattle-cluster-agent`.

Rancher deploys two agents on managed clusters: cattle-cluster-agent, a Deployment that connects to the cluster's Kubernetes API, and rancher-system-agent, a daemon on Rancher-provisioned RKE2/K3s nodes that applies plans for lifecycle operations such as Kubernetes upgrades and etcd snapshot create/restore.

To troubleshoot the Rancher server, check its pods with `kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher -o wide`, then use `kubectl -n cattle-system describe pods -l app=rancher`, `kubectl -n cattle-system logs -l app=rancher` and `kubectl -n cattle-system get events`.
command: kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher -o wide

fact: Fleet (SUSE Rancher Prime: Continuous Delivery) comes preinstalled in Rancher and is reached via ☰ > Continuous Delivery. The fleet-default workspace contains all downstream clusters registered through Rancher, fleet-local contains only the local cluster, and you can create your own workspaces.
Fleet can deploy raw Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize, or any combination from git; regardless of source, all resources are turned into Helm charts and Helm is used as the deployment engine.

Fleet does not fetch Helm chart dependencies: a chart in git must include them in its charts/ subdirectory, produced locally with `helm dependencies update $chart` (or `helm dependencies build $chart`) and committed.

Known issue: secrets referenced by Fleet GitRepos as clientSecretName and helmSecretName are not included in rancher-backup backups or restores. After a disaster-recovery restore or migration to a fresh cluster they must be recreated, or a ResourceSet modified to include them.

Fleet cannot be fully disabled in Rancher. The `continuous-delivery` feature flag (default true) disables only the GitOps continuous-delivery part: the gitjob deployment is no longer deployed to the local cluster and Continuous Delivery is hidden in the UI.

A project is a Rancher concept that groups namespaces; clusters contain projects and projects contain namespaces. In Rancher, user permissions are assigned at the project level and inherited by every namespace in the project. Each cluster gets a Default project and a System project, and the System project cannot be deleted.

Because kubectl cannot restrict namespace creation to a project, users with only project-scoped permissions should create namespaces through Rancher; a namespace created with kubectl may not be in their project and may be unusable for them.

Rancher's default global permissions are Administrator (full control of Rancher and all clusters), Standard User (can create and use clusters and grant others access to them) and User-Base (login access only). Users logging in through external authentication for the first time get the New User Default permissions, which is Standard User by default.

Cluster roles are Owner (full control of the cluster) and Member (view most cluster resources and create projects); project roles are Owner, Member and Read Only. Non-administrative users cannot access any cluster or project until an owner explicitly adds them as members.

The Rancher CLI authenticates with an API bearer token: `./rancher login https://<SERVER_URL> --token <BEARER_TOKEN>`; then select a project with `./rancher context switch`. The CLI binary is downloaded from ☰ > About > CLI Downloads.
The Rancher CLI cannot be used to install dashboard apps or Rancher feature charts; those are installed through Apps in the Rancher UI (or Helm).

API keys are created from User Avatar > Account & API Keys > Create API Key; they consist of an endpoint, access key, secret key and bearer token, are shown only once, and can be given an expiration (bounded by auth-token-max-ttl-minutes) and a cluster scope. An API key is required for the Rancher CLI.

On RKE2/K3s clusters with the authorized cluster endpoint (ACE) enabled (it must be enabled manually), the downloaded kubeconfig contains extra contexts for direct access without going through Rancher; with an FQDN defined, use `kubectl --context <CLUSTER_NAME>-fqdn get nodes`. SUSE recommends setting this up so the cluster stays reachable if Rancher is unavailable.

Helm chart repositories are added per cluster under Explore > Apps > Repositories > Create, as an http(s) Helm index URL, a Git repository containing charts, or (since v2.9.0) an OCI repository. Only Helm 3 compatible charts are supported, and Rancher syncs each repository every hour (3600 seconds) by default, configurable with refreshInterval.

Rancher Monitoring is installed per cluster from Explore > Cluster Tools > Monitoring and deploys into the cattle-monitoring-system namespace. It requires at least 1950Mi memory, 2700m CPU and 50Gi storage available, and port 9796 open on each node for Prometheus scraping.

In the current SUSE Rancher Prime docs, the rancher-monitoring (Monitoring v2) chart is deprecated and no longer receives updates; it is kept only for existing deployments, and new installations should use the decoupled rancher-monitoring-dashboards chart.

Rancher Logging is powered by the Logging operator, installed from the cluster's Apps (Logging app) into the cattle-logging-system namespace, and configured with Flows, ClusterFlows, Outputs and ClusterOutputs. It has two roles: logging-admin and logging-view.

If the Logging app hits 'Too many open files' or CrashLoopBackOff from inotify exhaustion, raise the kernel limits, e.g. `sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_instances=8192` and `sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288`.

If the Rancher server is deleted or unrecoverable, workloads in downstream clusters keep running. Registered clusters stay accessible as before, hosted clusters via the provider's credentials, and Rancher-provisioned RKE2/K3s clusters only if the authorized cluster endpoint was enabled and the kubeconfig downloaded beforehand. Rancher on Kubernetes is removed with the Rancher Cleanup tool.
An RKE2 server is installed with the install script from get.rke2.io, run as root or through sudo; it installs the rke2-server service and the rke2 binary.
After installing, the RKE2 server is enabled and started as the systemd unit rke2-server.service (agents use rke2-agent.service); the service restarts automatically after reboots or crashes.
An RKE2 agent (worker) is installed with the same script by setting INSTALL_RKE2_TYPE="agent", which installs the rke2-agent service.

An RKE2 agent joins a cluster through /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml containing `server: https://<server>:9345` and `token: <token from server node>`; port 9345 is the RKE2 supervisor registration port.
RKE2 reads its configuration from /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml by default; the file must be created manually, its keys map directly to CLI flags, and the service must be restarted after changes.
RKE2 writes an admin kubeconfig to /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml and installs kubectl, crictl and ctr in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin, which is not on the PATH by default.
To use kubectl or helm with RKE2, export KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml or pass --kubeconfig /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml.
If no token is set, the first RKE2 server generates one and stores it at /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/node-token; other servers and agents use it to register.
RKE2 server logs are followed with journalctl -u rke2-server -f (journalctl -u rke2-agent -f on agents).

RKE2 servers listen on TCP 9345 for node registration (supervisor API) and serve the Kubernetes API on TCP 6443; both must be reachable from other nodes and forwarded by a load balancer in front of the servers.

An HA RKE2 cluster uses an odd number of server nodes (three recommended) running etcd, behind a fixed registration address such as a layer 4 load balancer, round-robin DNS or a virtual IP, with that address added to tls-san.

Servers joining an RKE2 cluster fail with 'critical configuration value mismatch' when critical options differ between servers; agent-token, cluster-cidr, cluster-dns, cluster-domain, disable-cloud-controller, disable-kube-proxy, egress-selector-mode and service-cidr must be identical on all servers.
RKE2 server nodes are schedulable by default; to keep user workloads off them, taint them with node-taint `CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoExecute` in config.yaml.
Every RKE2 node needs a unique node name, which defaults to the hostname; if hostnames collide, change the hostname, set node-name in config.yaml, or set with-node-id: true to append a random ID.

To use RKE2's bundled crictl, export CRI_CONFIG_FILE=/var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/etc/crictl.yaml and run /var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin/crictl; the containerd socket is /run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock.

On hosts with NetworkManager, configure it to ignore CNI-managed interfaces with /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/rke2-canal.conf (keyfile unmanaged-devices for flannel*, cali*, tunl* and related interfaces), and disable nm-cloud-setup.service and nm-cloud-setup.timer if present.

RKE2 installed by tarball is removed with /usr/local/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh (RPM installs: /usr/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh; read-only or btrfs roots: /opt/rke2/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh); uninstalling deletes the cluster data.

RKE2 combines K3s's usability and deployment model with RKE1's close alignment to upstream Kubernetes; it does not rely on Docker, runs control plane components as static pods managed by the kubelet, and embeds containerd. It targets security and compliance, with defaults for the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark and FIPS 140-2 compliance.

RKE2 takes scheduled etcd snapshots by default at 00:00 and 12:00 system time (cron 0 */12 * * *), keeping 5 per server node, stored under /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/snapshots; etcd-snapshot-schedule-cron and etcd-snapshot-retention change this.
An on-demand RKE2 etcd snapshot is taken with rke2 etcd-snapshot save on a server node; on-demand snapshots are named on-demand-<node>-<timestamp> and have no automatic retention.

Snapshots across all RKE2 cluster members can be listed with kubectl get etcdsnapshotfile (cluster-scoped ETCDSnapshotFile resources); rke2 etcd-snapshot list only shows snapshots visible to the node it runs on.
Old on-demand RKE2 snapshots are pruned with rke2 etcd-snapshot prune --snapshot-retention <NUM-OF-SNAPSHOTS-TO-RETAIN>; specific snapshots are removed with rke2 etcd-snapshot delete <SNAPSHOT-NAME>.

To restore an RKE2 etcd snapshot, stop rke2-server, run rke2 server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=<PATH-TO-SNAPSHOT>, wait for the message to restart without --cluster-reset, then start rke2-server again.

When restoring a snapshot in a multi-server RKE2 cluster, stop RKE2 on all servers, restore on one server, start it, then on each other server delete /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/ before starting it so it rejoins the restored cluster.

Restoring an RKE2 snapshot to a different host requires the original server token from /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/token, passed with --token (or set in config.yaml), because the token decrypts the bootstrap data in the snapshot.

RKE2 can upload etcd snapshots to S3-compatible storage with --etcd-s3 plus options such as --etcd-s3-bucket, --etcd-s3-endpoint, --etcd-s3-access-key and --etcd-s3-secret-key; --etcd-s3-retention (default 5) applies cluster-wide, and an S3 config Secret cannot be used during a restore.
Upgrade RKE2 server nodes first, one at a time, then agent nodes, and do not skip intermediate Kubernetes minor versions because the version skew policy applies.
RKE2 is upgraded to a specific version by re-running the install script with INSTALL_RKE2_VERSION=vX.Y.Z+rke2rN (add INSTALL_RKE2_TYPE=agent on agents), then restarting rke2-server or rke2-agent.

Automated RKE2 upgrades use Rancher's system-upgrade-controller, installed with kubectl apply of its crd.yaml and system-upgrade-controller.yaml, plus Plan resources (a server plan and an agent plan) in the system-upgrade namespace using the rancher/rke2-upgrade image.

If an RKE2 cluster is managed by SUSE Rancher Prime (Rancher), manage upgrades through Rancher: provisioned clusters are upgraded by Rancher's system agent, and imported clusters have their system-upgrade-controller and plans managed by Rancher unless version management is disabled.

RKE2 bundles the Canal, Cilium, Calico and Flannel CNI plugins (plus Multus as a secondary plugin); Canal is the default, the plugin is chosen with the cni key in config.yaml (or none), and the primary CNI cannot be changed on a running cluster.

Bundled RKE2 CNI charts (named rke2-<cni> in kube-system) are customised with a HelmChartConfig of the same name and namespace, placed in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests, for example rke2-canal-config.yaml.

Starting with RKE2 v1.36, Traefik is the default ingress controller for new clusters; earlier versions deploy ingress-nginx (rke2-ingress-nginx). The ingress-controller config key selects none, traefik or ingress-nginx, and the first value listed becomes the default ingress class.

RKE2 reads private registry and mirror settings from /etc/rancher/rke2/registries.yaml at startup (top-level keys mirrors and configs); the file must exist on every node that pulls from the registry, including schedulable servers, and RKE2 must be restarted after changes.

For RKE2 image pull failures, check the containerd log at /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/containerd/containerd.log, because the kubelet error may only show the final attempt against the default endpoint; containerd always tries the default endpoint last unless disable-default-registry-endpoint: true is set.

For an RKE2 air-gap install without a private registry, copy the release's images archive (for example rke2-images.linux-amd64.tar.zst) into /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/images/ on each node; RKE2 imports archives in that directory at startup.

install.sh runs offline on an air-gapped RKE2 node when INSTALL_RKE2_ARTIFACT_PATH points to a directory holding the pre-downloaded install.sh, rke2.linux-amd64.tar.gz, rke2-images.linux-amd64.tar.zst and sha256sum-amd64.txt, for example INSTALL_RKE2_ARTIFACT_PATH=/root/rke2-artifacts sh install.sh.

RKE2 needs a default route to auto-detect the node's primary IP and for kube-proxy ClusterIP routing; on nodes without one (common in air-gapped networks), add a route even via a dummy interface before RKE2 starts.

For CIS hardening, RKE2 ships a sysctl file the operator must apply: on tarball installs copy /usr/local/share/rke2/rke2-cis-sysctl.conf to /etc/sysctl.d/60-rke2-cis.conf (RPM installs: /usr/share/rke2/rke2-cis-sysctl.conf) and restart systemd-sysctl, on fresh installs only.

With a CIS profile, RKE2 requires an etcd user and group on the host (it exits if missing); create them with sudo useradd -r -c "etcd user" -s /sbin/nologin -M etcd -U, defined in /etc/passwd and /etc/group.

On RKE2 v1.29 and newer, CIS hardening is enabled with profile: "cis" in /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml; it checks host requirements, runs etcd as the etcd user, applies network policies, tightens file permissions, and enforces Pod Security Admission restricted mode in all namespaces except kube-system, compliance-operator-system and tigera-operator.

Files placed in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests on server nodes are deployed automatically like kubectl apply, at startup and when changed; packaged components can be removed with the disable option (for example rke2-metrics-server), and deleting a file does not delete its resources.

K3s is installed as a service on systemd or openrc systems with the script at get.k3s.io; it also installs kubectl, crictl, ctr, k3s-killall.sh and k3s-uninstall.sh and writes a kubeconfig to /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml.

A K3s agent joins by running the install script with K3S_URL (the server on port 6443) and K3S_TOKEN; setting K3S_URL makes the installer configure an agent, and the token is in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token on the server.

K3s reads its config file from /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml (plus drop-ins in /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml.d/*.yaml), and its admin kubeconfig is /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml, which the bundled kubectl uses automatically; the RKE2 equivalents are /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml and /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml.

Options passed to the K3s install script (INSTALL_K3S_EXEC, K3S_ variables, trailing arguments) are persisted into the service, but are lost if not repeated when the script is re-run; to keep configuration independent of the installer, use /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml.

An HA K3s cluster with embedded etcd starts by installing the first server with a shared token and --cluster-init; additional servers join with the same token and --server https://<server1>:6443, keeping an odd number of servers (three or more).

K3s uses embedded SQLite by default, which cannot be used with multiple servers; an existing single-node SQLite cluster can be converted to embedded etcd by restarting the K3s server with --cluster-init.

K3s serves both its supervisor and the Kubernetes API on TCP 6443 (there is no separate 9345 port as in RKE2); nodes also need UDP 8472 for Flannel VXLAN, TCP 10250 for kubelet metrics, and TCP 2379-2380 between servers for embedded etcd HA.

K3s etcd snapshots work like RKE2's: scheduled snapshots at 00:00 and 12:00 with 5 retained per node, and on-demand snapshots taken with k3s etcd-snapshot save, stored under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/snapshots.

To restore a K3s etcd snapshot, stop K3s (systemctl stop k3s), run k3s server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=<PATH-TO-SNAPSHOT>, then start K3s again; in multi-server clusters, delete /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/ on the other servers before restarting them.

K3s uses Flannel as its CNI with the vxlan backend by default; --flannel-backend=wireguard-native adds encryption, and to use another CNI start K3s with --flannel-backend=none (and usually --disable-network-policy). Flannel options are set on servers and must match on all of them.

K3s packaged components (coredns, traefik, local-storage, metrics-server, plus the servicelb controller) are deployed from /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests and can be removed with --disable, for example --disable=traefik.

For a K3s air-gap install, place k3s-airgap-images-amd64.tar.zst in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/images/, put the matching k3s binary in /usr/local/bin, and run the downloaded script with INSTALL_K3S_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true ./install.sh.

K3s reads private registry configuration from /etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml at startup, using the same mirrors and configs format as RKE2's /etc/rancher/rke2/registries.yaml; it is needed on each node that pulls from the registry, including schedulable servers.

K3s is upgraded by re-running the install script with the original options, optionally pinning INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=vX.Y.Z+k3s1; the script downloads the new binary and restarts K3s, upgrading servers one at a time before agents.

K3s installed by the script is removed with /usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh on servers and /usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh on agents; this deletes the local datastore, local-storage volume data and node configuration.

SUSE Storage is derived from the upstream Longhorn project; the documentation uses the SUSE Storage name, but Kubernetes resources, Helm charts and CLI tools keep the longhorn nomenclature, such as the longhorn-system namespace, the longhorn.io API group, longhorn-manager and longhorn-engine.

SUSE Storage has a control plane and a data plane: the Longhorn Manager (control plane) runs on every node as a Kubernetes DaemonSet and creates and manages volumes, while the Longhorn Engine (data plane) is a dedicated storage controller created for each volume.
The Longhorn Engine for a volume always runs on the same node as the pod that uses the volume, and it synchronously replicates the volume across multiple replicas stored on multiple nodes.

The Instance Manager is a per-node pod in the longhorn-system namespace (one per data engine version) that hosts the engine and replica instances for many volumes; there is no separate per-volume engine pod, so the instance-manager pod is what you target when debugging engine or replica behavior.
A SUSE Storage volume with a replica count of N can tolerate at most N-1 replica failures, because at least one healthy replica is needed for the volume to remain operational.

SUSE Storage volumes are thin-provisioned and only use the space they need, but a volume's actual size on disk does not shrink when files are deleted, because SUSE Storage works at the block level and does not know the file system removed the content.

SUSE Storage snapshots are stored locally as part of each replica on the cluster nodes' disks, while backups are objects in a backupstore, an NFS or S3-compatible store external to the Kubernetes cluster, so data can be retrieved even if the cluster is unavailable.

SUSE Storage backups are incremental: each new backup of a volume transmits only changed blocks, and backup operations use 2 MB blocks, so if any 4K block within a 2 MB boundary changes, the whole 2 MB block is backed up.
For SUSE Storage, the StorageClass provisioner is always driver.longhorn.io (provisioner: driver.longhorn.io), the name of the Longhorn CSI driver.
The StorageClass parameter numberOfReplicas (for example numberOfReplicas: "3") sets the number of replicas for volumes provisioned from it; the default is 3 and the value must be between 1 and 20.

The dataLocality StorageClass parameter (for example dataLocality: "best-effort") accepts disabled (default), best-effort and strict-local; best-effort tries to keep a replica on the workload's node without failing the volume, while strict-local keeps the only replica local, requires a replica count of 1 and is incompatible with RWX volumes.

SUSE Storage StorageClass parameters override global settings and apply only when new volumes are created; if a StorageClass is modified, changes are not propagated to volumes previously created with it.

The diskSelector and nodeSelector StorageClass parameters (for example diskSelector: "ssd,fast") take comma-separated storage tags that restrict which disks and nodes can hold replicas; when several tags are specified, the disk and its node must have all of them.

The dataEngine StorageClass parameter selects the data engine; it defaults to "v1", and dataEngine: "v2" provisions V2 Data Engine volumes, which requires the V2 Data Engine to be enabled and block-type disks to be available.

SUSE Storage provides ReadWriteMany (RWX) volumes by exposing regular Longhorn volumes through NFSv4.1 servers running in share-manager-<volume-name> pods in the longhorn-system namespace, so every node that mounts an RWX volume needs an NFSv4 client installed.

On SUSE and openSUSE nodes the NFSv4 client needed for RWX volumes and NFS backups is installed with zypper install nfs-client; Debian and Ubuntu use apt-get install nfs-common and RHEL/CentOS use yum install nfs-utils.

Mount options for generic RWX volumes are customized with the nfsOptions StorageClass parameter (for example nfsOptions: "vers=4.2,noresvport,softerr,timeo=600,retrans=5"); by default SUSE Storage mounts RWX volumes with NFS 4.1, softerr, timeo=600 and retrans=5, and when you set nfsOptions you must supply the complete set of options because SUSE Storage does not validate the string.

Migratable RWX volumes are for live migration of virtualized workloads such as KubeVirt VMs; they require volumeMode: Block, the ReadWriteMany access mode and a StorageClass with migratable: "true", and they are not intended for general shared file system use.

SUSE Storage supports the ReadWriteOnce, ReadWriteOncePod and ReadWriteMany access modes; ReadOnlyMany (ROX) is not supported, and for read-only access from multiple pods you use ReadWriteMany with read-only mount options in the pod spec.

V1 Data Engine volumes use iSCSI, so open-iscsi must be installed on each node; on SUSE and openSUSE install it with zypper install open-iscsi and then enable and start iscsid with systemctl enable iscsid and systemctl start iscsid.
Nodes must not use open-iscsi 2.1.12, because a breaking configuration change in that upstream release causes volume attachment failures; use open-iscsi 2.1.11 or earlier, or 2.1.13 or later.

The iscsi_tcp kernel module must be loaded before the iscsid service starts (modprobe iscsi_tcp); on SUSE and openSUSE this module is only in the kernel-default package, so a system with kernel-default-base must switch to kernel-default.

The Longhorn CLI longhornctl checks node prerequisites with ./longhornctl check preflight (adding --enable-spdk to also validate V2 Data Engine requirements), and can install them with longhornctl install preflight.

Nodes hosting V2 Data Engine volumes need an AMD64 CPU with SSE4.2 or an ARM64 CPU, the kernel modules vfio_pci, uio_pci_generic and nvme-tcp, 2 GiB of 2 MiB huge pages (1024 pages), raw block disks (local NVMe strongly recommended), and Linux kernel 6.7 or later is recommended for NVMe/TCP support and stability.

To allocate the 1024 2 MiB huge pages SPDK needs on a node temporarily, run echo 1024 > /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages; this is not persistent, so for persistence add hugepagesz=2M hugepages=1024 to the kernel boot parameters and verify with grep Huge /proc/meminfo.

The V2 Data Engine is enabled after installation by setting the v2-data-engine setting to true (UI: Settings > V2 Data Engine); the instance-manager pods then restart automatically, and SUSE Storage blocks changing this setting while volumes are attached.

SUSE Storage recommends enabling only one data engine (V1 or V2) per cluster, because with both enabled each node runs separate V1 and V2 instance-manager pods with their own CPU reservations, and each V2 instance-manager pod typically consumes one dedicated CPU core due to spdk_tgt polling.

SUSE Storage has two disk types tied to the data engines: filesystem-type disks (an extent-based file system such as ext4 or XFS mounted on the host) for V1 volumes and raw block-type disks for V2 volumes; when a node is added, a default filesystem-type disk is created at /var/lib/longhorn.

The V2 Data Engine is generally available as of SUSE Storage v1.12.0 and described as suitable for production use in supported environments, while storage sharding (erasure coding on V2), introduced in v1.12.1, is experimental and not recommended for production.
In the V1 and V2 feature parity matrix, data locality disabled and best-effort are supported on both engines, but strict-local data locality is supported only on V1 and not on V2.

SUSE Storage upgrades are supported only from one minor version to the next consecutive minor version (for example v1.11.x to v1.12), patch upgrades within a minor are supported, skipping a minor version fails automatically, and downgrades are not supported.

SUSE Storage installed from the SUSE Application Collection OCI chart is upgraded with helm upgrade longhorn oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/suse-storage --namespace longhorn-system --version <version> --set global.imagePullSecrets=<PULL_IMAGE_SECRET>, passing the target version and the image pull secret.

Before upgrading SUSE Storage, detach all V2 Data Engine volumes (V2 does not support live upgrades), avoid upgrading while any volume is Faulted, avoid upgrading with a failed BackingImage, and create a Longhorn system backup.

After upgrading the Longhorn Manager, volume engines must also be upgraded; this can be done manually in the UI (Upgrade Engine) or automatically via the Concurrent Automatic Engine Upgrade Per Node Limit setting, whose default 0 disables automatic engine upgrades and for which 3 is the recommended value.

To confirm that a SUSE Storage installation or upgrade succeeded, run kubectl -n longhorn-system get pod and check that pods such as longhorn-manager, longhorn-ui, longhorn-driver-deployer, longhorn-csi-plugin, the csi-* sidecars, instance-manager and engine-image are Running.

An AWS S3 backup target URL has the form s3://<your-bucket-name>@<your-aws-region>/; it must end with a slash or an error occurs, the region must be included, and an optional subdirectory prefix can follow.

S3 credentials for a backup target are stored in a Kubernetes secret with AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, created with kubectl create secret generic <aws-secret> --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<your-aws-access-key-id> --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<your-aws-secret-access-key> -n longhorn-system; it must be in the longhorn-system namespace for SUSE Storage to access it.

An NFS backup target uses a URL such as nfs://longhorn-test-nfs-svc.default:/opt/backupstore; the NFS server must support NFSv4, the default mount options are actimeo=1,soft,timeo=300,retry=2, and custom options are appended with the nfsOptions query parameter.

The lifecycle of Longhorn backups in the backupstore is managed entirely by SUSE Storage, so retention policies must not be applied directly on the backupstore; retention is configured with recurring jobs instead.

Recurring jobs are RecurringJob custom resources (longhorn.io/v1beta2) in longhorn-system with cron, task, retain, concurrency and optional groups and labels; tasks are backup, backup-force-create, snapshot, snapshot-force-create, snapshot-cleanup, snapshot-delete and filesystem-trim, and a job in the default group applies to volumes that have no recurring job.

A recurring job is attached to a Longhorn volume with kubectl -n longhorn-system label volume/<VOLUME-NAME> recurring-job.longhorn.io/<RECURRING-JOB-NAME>=enabled (or recurring-job-group.longhorn.io/<GROUP-NAME>=enabled for a group), and removed by deleting the label with a trailing dash.

Recurring job labels on a PVC have no effect by default; the PVC must first be labeled as the source with kubectl -n <NAMESPACE> label pvc/<PVC-NAME> recurring-job.longhorn.io/source=enabled, after which SUSE Storage periodically syncs the PVC's recurring job labels to the volume, overriding the volume's own recurring job labels.

Recurring jobs can be assigned to all future volumes of a StorageClass with the recurringJobSelector parameter (for example recurringJobSelector: '[{"name":"backup", "isGroup":true}]'), a JSON list whose entries give the name of an existing recurring job or group and isGroup true or false.

A disaster recovery (DR) volume is a standby volume in a secondary cluster, created from a backup of the primary volume; both clusters must use the same backup target, the DR volume polls and incrementally restores newer backups, stays unmounted until it is manually activated, and cannot have snapshots, backups, PVs or PVCs created before activation.

A DR volume can be activated when it is healthy, or when degraded only if the Allow Volume Creation with Degraded Availability setting is enabled; with that setting disabled, activating a degraded DR volume leaves it stuck in the Attached state.

To create Longhorn backups through the Kubernetes CSI VolumeSnapshot API, use a VolumeSnapshotClass with driver driver.longhorn.io and the parameter type: bak; a VolumeSnapshot using that class creates a backup, and the VolumeSnapshotContent snapshotHandle has the form bak://backup-volume/backup-name.

Reverting a SUSE Storage volume to a snapshot requires the volume to be attached in maintenance mode, which attaches it without enabling the frontend (block device or iSCSI) so the data cannot be accessed or modified during the revert.

To add a filesystem-type disk with kubectl, mount the formatted disk on the host and run kubectl edit node.longhorn.io <node-name> to add an entry under spec.disks with its path, diskType: filesystem and allowScheduling; for alternative paths use mount --bind rather than a symbolic link, and keep the mount in /etc/fstab.
SUSE Storage refuses to add a block-type disk for V2 that contains an existing file system or partition table, so the device must first be cleaned with wipefs -a /path/to/block/device.

Storage Minimal Available Percentage (default 25) is the minimum available space a disk must keep before new replicas are scheduled and Storage Over Provisioning Percentage (default 100) caps scheduled size relative to usable space; on the root disk keep 25 and 100, and on a dedicated disk the minimal available percentage can be lowered to 10.

SUSE Storage settings can be changed from the command line with kubectl edit settings.longhorn.io <SETTING-NAME> -n longhorn-system; use settings.longhorn.io (or lhs) rather than the bare name settings to avoid collisions with other CRDs.

Node Drain Policy defaults to block-if-contains-last-replica, so SUSE Storage blocks a node drain while the node holds the last healthy replica of a volume; drains also need --ignore-daemonsets, and options such as allow-if-replica-is-stopped or evicting the replica let the drain finish.

When a node goes down, pods of StatefulSets and Deployments get stuck Terminating and their RWO Longhorn volumes stay attached; the Pod Deletion Policy When Node is Down setting (default do-nothing) can force-delete those pods (delete-statefulset-pod, delete-deployment-pod or delete-both-statefulset-and-deployment-pod) so the volumes are released and replacements start elsewhere.

Most SUSE Storage logs and configuration can be collected with the Generate Support Bundle link at the bottom of the UI, which downloads a zip file of SUSE Storage-related configuration and logs; dmesg is not included and must be retrieved from each node separately.

If an RWX volume fails to mount with an error mentioning that you might need a /sbin/mount.<type> helper program, the node is missing the NFSv4 client, which must be installed on every node that mounts RWX volumes.

The Default Replica Count setting (default 3) applies to volumes created from the SUSE Storage UI; the recommendation is 3 replicas when there are three or more storage nodes and 2 otherwise, while a single replica works on a single-node cluster but without high availability.

SUSE Storage uninstallation fails unless the deleting-confirmation-flag setting is set to true; after removing workloads that use SUSE Storage volumes, a Helm installation is removed with helm uninstall longhorn -n longhorn-system.

Default disks for new nodes can be defined with the node label node.longhorn.io/create-default-disk: 'config' plus a node.longhorn.io/default-disks-config annotation describing the disks in JSON; this requires the Create Default Disk on Labeled Nodes setting to be enabled and only takes effect when the node has no existing disks or tags.

Replica Node Level Soft Anti-Affinity defaults to false, which prevents SUSE Storage from scheduling a replica on a node that already has a healthy replica of the same volume; replicas therefore need separate nodes unless the setting is enabled.

When all replicas of a volume become faulty, for example after a network disconnection, the Automatic Salvage setting (default true) makes SUSE Storage identify the usable replicas and use them for the volume; separately, Replica Replenishment Wait Interval (default 600 seconds) is how long SUSE Storage waits to reuse a failed replica's data before creating a new replica for a degraded volume.

SUSE Virtualization (project name Harvester) is a hyperconverged infrastructure solution that runs on bare metal and is built on Kubernetes. It uses KubeVirt (KVM) for virtualization management, SUSE Storage (Longhorn) as its built-in distributed block storage, an immutable SUSE Linux Micro based operating system, and Grafana and Prometheus for observability.
SUSE Virtualization v1.8.x uses KubeVirt v1.7, SUSE Storage (Longhorn) v1.11, SUSE Rancher Prime v2.14, RKE2 v1.35 and SUSE Linux Micro 6.2.

Production SUSE Virtualization nodes need at least 16 CPU cores (AMD64 or ARM64 with hardware-assisted virtualization), 64 GB of memory, 500 GB of disk (1 TB or more recommended) and 10 Gbps Ethernet. Development/testing minimums are 8 cores, 32 GB memory, 250 GB disk and 1 Gbps Ethernet.
Each SUSE Virtualization disk should deliver 5,000+ random IOPS (SSD/NVMe), management node storage must meet etcd speed requirements, and only local disks and hardware RAID are supported.

Starting with v1.8.0, new SUSE Virtualization installations are only possible on UEFI systems (legacy BIOS was deprecated in v1.7.0). Mixed-architecture clusters are not supported, and nested virtualization is not supported for guest VMs.

Use CPUs with the same specifications on all SUSE Virtualization nodes, because live migration checks CPU compatibility and blocks migration between incompatible hosts. Each node must also have a unique product_uuid (/sys/class/dmi/id/product_uuid).

A SUSE Virtualization HA cluster needs three nodes: the first node is a management node, and once there are three or more nodes the next two that join are promoted to management nodes. With three management nodes, the cluster tolerates the failure of one node.

The SUSE Virtualization ISO installer offers three modes: create a new cluster, join an existing cluster (needs the cluster VIP and cluster token), or install binaries only. Joining nodes choose a role: Default, Management, Witness or Worker.

A SUSE Virtualization node's IP address cannot be changed during the cluster's lifecycle. If you use DHCP, the server must always give the node the same IP, and the DHCP configuration must include the routers option so the host gets a default route.

The SUSE Virtualization management VIP must be different from every node IP, must be in the same subnet as the node management interfaces, and all management interfaces must be on the same layer-2 segment because the VIP relies on ARP. When the VIP comes from DHCP, configure a static MAC-to-IP mapping.
To get the MAC address of the SUSE Virtualization VIP, run on a management node: kubectl get svc -n kube-system ingress-expose -ojsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.kube-vip\.io/hwaddr}'

To find which SUSE Virtualization node currently holds the VIP, run: kubectl -n kube-system get svc ingress-expose -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.kube-vip\.io/vipHost}'. Alternatively, run ip address show mgmt-br on each management node and look for the VIP.
To log in to a SUSE Virtualization node over SSH, use the rancher user: ssh rancher@node-ip. The rancher user can run privileged commands with sudo without a password.
The SUSE Virtualization kubeconfig can be downloaded from the Support page of the UI, or read on a management node as root with: cat /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml

To reset a forgotten SUSE Virtualization administrator password, SSH to a management node, switch to root and run: kubectl -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password
command: kubectl -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password

fact: To check SUSE Virtualization control-plane readiness, query the readyz endpoint with the cluster token and the real VIP: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://$VIP/v1/harvester/readyz (add -k for self-signed certificates). A healthy cluster returns {"ready":true,...}.

SUSE Virtualization automatically creates a built-in cluster network named mgmt, which is always enabled on all hosts and cannot be disabled or deleted. Custom cluster networks isolate VM traffic; each needs at least one network configuration with a node selector, uplink NICs and bond options (default active-backup), and all configurations in a custom cluster network must use the same MTU.

SUSE Virtualization VM networks are created under Networks > VM Networks. Types include the management network, VLAN networks (type L2VlanNetwork, mode Access, with a VLAN ID and cluster network), untagged networks, and, from v1.7.0, VLAN trunk networks (L2VlanNetwork, mode Trunk, with a VLAN ID range). Uplink switch ports must be configured as trunk ports.

By default, a VM's management network IP in SUSE Virtualization is reachable only from the cluster nodes and changes after the VM reboots; use a VLAN or untagged network when VMs need external access. VM interfaces on mgmt have an MTU of 1450 because of the Calico and Flannel overlay overhead.

If the mgmt MTU was set to a value other than 0 or 1500 during installation, annotate the mgmt cluster network after deployment so VM networks inherit it, for example: kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000". The value must match the installed mtu, and all nodes must use the same MTU.

VMs are created on the SUSE Virtualization Virtual Machines page: choose single or multiple instances, a namespace (only harvester-public is visible to all users) and a name, then set CPU, memory and SSH keys on the Basics tab, the image and disks on the Volumes tab (the first disk is the root disk), networks on the Networks tab (the management network is added by default), and cloud-init and run strategy under Advanced Options.

SUSE Virtualization VMs use a run strategy: RerunOnFailure is the default (respawn only after failure; a clean guest shutdown is not restarted), Always (always respawned), Manual (controlled only by start/stop/restart actions), and Stop (no VM instance).

SUSE Virtualization images can be created by downloading from a URL reachable by the cluster, uploading a local file (qcow2, raw and ISO are supported), or exporting a volume (Export Image on the Volumes page). Avoid daily-build URLs, because Longhorn re-downloads the URL to self-heal lost backing-image replicas and a changed file causes a checksum mismatch.

If the SUSE Virtualization UI shows no IP for a VM, check whether the QEMU guest agent is reporting by running: kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'. If the output lacks guest-agent, the qemu-guest-agent package is not installed; enable Install guest agent in the VM's Cloud Config.

cloud-init runs only on a VM's first boot. After changing Cloud Config (for example selecting Install guest agent) on an existing VM, delete the cloud-init directory inside the guest with sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/* and restart the VM so cloud-init runs again.

To live-migrate a VM in SUSE Virtualization, go to the Virtual Machines page, select ⋮ > Migrate, choose the target node and click Apply. A running or pending migration can be stopped with ⋮ > Abort Migration. The Migrate option is unavailable when the cluster has only one node, the VM is non-migratable, or a migration is already running or pending.

A SUSE Virtualization VM is non-migratable if it uses host device passthrough (PCI, vGPU, USB), has a node selector binding it to a specific node, or has scheduling rules that match only one node (for example a cluster network covering one node, or CPU pinning with CPU Manager enabled on only one node). Non-migratable VMs must be shut down for maintenance.

SUSE Virtualization aborts a live migration that exceeds the completion timeout (150 seconds per GiB of data by default, so an 8 GiB VM times out after 1200 seconds) or makes no memory-copy progress for 150 seconds. Change these with the completionTimeoutPerGiB and progressTimeout fields of the kubevirt-migration setting, or enable allowAutoConverge to throttle busy guests.

From v1.7.0, configure SUSE Virtualization live migration only through the kubevirt-migration setting, not by editing the kubevirt object. The whole JSON value is written to spec.configuration.migrations, overwriting direct edits. Do not change the setting while migrations are in progress.

When nodes have different host CPU models, SUSE Virtualization VMs using the default host-model can only migrate to nodes with the same model. Set a CPU model supported by all nodes cluster-wide with kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system (add spec.configuration.cpuModel), or per VM with spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.model; both require restarting the VMs.

Maintenance Mode (host ⋮ > Enable Maintenance Mode) evicts all VMs from a SUSE Virtualization node using batch live migration and needs at least two active nodes. The VM label harvesterhci.io/maintain-mode-strategy overrides the behavior per VM: Migrate (default), ShutdownAndRestartAfterEnable, ShutdownAndRestartAfterDisable or Shutdown.

VM backups in SUSE Virtualization are stored on a backup target, which is an NFS server or an S3-compatible server configured at Settings > backup-target. Backup support is limited to SUSE Storage (Longhorn) volumes; volumes in external storage cannot be backed up.

In SUSE Virtualization, Take Backup copies VM volumes to the backup target, and the backup can restore a new VM (including on another cluster that uses the same backup target) or replace an existing VM, which must be powered off. Take VM Snapshot keeps the snapshot inside the cluster and does not need a backup target.

Before backing up or snapshotting an Ubuntu (later than 16.04) VM managed by netplan, set dhcp-identifier: mac in its network configuration. Otherwise the restored VM keeps the original machine ID and receives the same DHCP IP address, which causes conflicts.

SUSE Virtualization (v1.4.0+) schedules VM backups or snapshots from the Virtual Machine Schedules screen (Create Schedule) with a type, VM, cron expression, Retain count and Max Failure count. The interval must be at least one hour, schedules are suspended after Max Failure consecutive failures, and Longhorn recurring snapshot/backup jobs are not supported.

SUSE Virtualization freezes guest filesystems through KubeVirt virt-freezer and the QEMU guest agent during backups and snapshots. To test compatibility, exec into the VM's virt-launcher compute container and run virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>, then always thaw with virt-freezer --unfreeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>.

SUSE Virtualization does not support downgrades. Upgrades move at most one minor version at a time (for example v1.7.x to v1.8.x, or to a later patch in the same minor), and if Rancher manages the cluster, Rancher must be upgraded first. Upgrades start from the Upgrade button on the Dashboard.
Before upgrading SUSE Virtualization, every node needs at least 30 GiB of free system partition space, checked with df -h /usr/local/. Upgrades are denied if any node has less.

If a SUSE Virtualization upgrade fails with 'Node xxx will reach xx.xx% storage space after loading new images. It's higher than kubelet image garbage collection threshold 85%.', run crictl rmi --prune on the node to remove unused images before starting a new upgrade.

In the SUSE Virtualization upgrade-config setting, restoreVM controls non-migratable VMs during upgrades: with false (default), you must stop non-migratable VMs in multi-node clusters for the upgrade to proceed and they are not restarted; with true, they are shut down and automatically restarted after the upgrade completes. Live-migratable VMs are moved by batch migration.

To stop an ongoing SUSE Virtualization upgrade, log in to a control-plane node as root, list the upgrade with kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true, delete that Upgrade CR, and resume any paused ManagedCharts. Generate a support bundle first.

During the node-upgrade phase (Phase 4) of a SUSE Virtualization upgrade, check the per-node pre-drain and post-drain jobs with kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node. If the upgrade fails or is stuck in Phase 4, do not restart it unless SUSE Support instructs you to.

A SUSE Virtualization witness node only acts as an etcd member to keep quorum and stores no data. A cluster can have only one witness node, the witness role can be assigned only when the node joins the cluster, and the supported layout is two management nodes plus one witness (optionally with worker nodes). The 180 GB disk minimum applies to witness nodes.

In a SUSE Virtualization cluster of two management nodes plus one witness node (no workers), create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2, because the default harvester-longhorn StorageClass uses 3 replicas and volumes would be Degraded. With one or more worker nodes, the existing default StorageClass can be used.
When selecting a migration target in SUSE Virtualization, the target list can include the witness node. Do not select the witness node as the migration target, because the migration will fail.

PCI passthrough in SUSE Virtualization requires enabling the pcidevices-controller add-on. Then select devices on Advanced > PCI Devices and click Enable Passthrough, attach them through the VM's Edit Config > PCI Devices, and restart the VM. The device is bound to vfio-pci so the guest uses its own drivers. Do not pass through host-owned devices such as management or VLAN NICs.

SUSE Virtualization supports NVIDIA SR-IOV vGPUs through the pcidevices-controller add-on together with the nvidia-driver-toolkit add-on. Enable the GPU on Advanced > SR-IOV GPU Devices, choose a profile on the vGPU Devices screen, and attach the vGPU to a VM. Starting with v1.8.0, vGPUs are attached as normal PCI devices: pass through the PCIDevice with the same name as the VGPUDevice.

To manage SUSE Virtualization from Rancher, open Virtualization Management in the Rancher UI, select Import Existing, enter a cluster name and click Create, then follow the registration guide in the SUSE Virtualization UI (it sets the cluster-registration-url setting). All nodes must reach TCP port 443 on the Rancher load balancer, and a cattle-cluster-agent pod that pulls the rancher-agent image is created.

For production, install the Rancher server that manages SUSE Virtualization on a dedicated, high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes. Do not install Rancher with Docker in production; that is only for quick evaluation. For testing, Rancher can be installed with Helm in a VM on SUSE Virtualization.

Rancher provisions guest RKE2 or K3s clusters on SUSE Virtualization with the Harvester node driver, which is enabled by default. Create a Harvester cloud credential (Cluster Management > Cloud Credentials > Create > Harvester > Imported Harvester Cluster), then create the cluster with the Harvester node driver. The node driver supports only cloud images, needs a VLAN network (with DHCP or the Managed DHCP add-on), and integrates the Harvester cloud provider (load balancers) and CSI driver.

Since Harvester node driver v0.6.3, qemu-guest-agent is no longer injected automatically. If the cloud image lacks it, add it in the node driver User Data (cloud-config with packages: qemu-guest-agent and systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service); otherwise the guest cluster is not provisioned successfully.

A SUSE Virtualization VM can become Unschedulable because of an automatically applied affinity rule, for example network.harvesterhci.io/<cluster-network> when the VM uses a cluster network that no active node has set up. The fix is to make sure active nodes have that cluster network configured so they carry the label.

If the Start button is missing in the SUSE Virtualization UI for a VM that is Off, because its virt-launcher pod completed but the VM still has a pending Start request, force delete the pod: kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force. The Start button then reappears.
SUSE Security (project name NeuVector) runs as four types of security containers: Controller, Enforcer, Manager and Scanner. An Updater container is also used to refresh the CVE database.

The Controller manages the cluster of Enforcers and provides the REST APIs used by the management console. Multiple Controllers in a high-availability configuration are recommended; 3 Controllers is the default in the Kubernetes production sample.
The Enforcer is a lightweight container that enforces the security policies. One Enforcer should be deployed on each node (host), for example as a DaemonSet.

The Manager is a stateless container that provides the web UI console (HTTPS only) for managing SUSE Security. It is not recommended to scale more than one Manager behind a load balancer because of potential session state issues.

The Scanner performs vulnerability and compliance scanning for images, containers and nodes. It is typically deployed as a replicaset that can be scaled up; the Controller assigns scanning jobs to available scanners in a round-robin fashion.

The Updater refreshes the CVE database by restarting the scanner deployment so that the latest scanner image (which contains the newest CVE database) is pulled. The sample deployments run it as a cron job every day at midnight (schedule "0 0 * * *").
Controllers use the consensus-based RAFT protocol to elect a leader, so the number of active Controllers should be an odd number such as 3, 5 or 7.

Documented minimum sizing: Controller 1 vCPU and 2GB memory (min 1 instance, 3 for HA, odd numbers only); Enforcer 1+ vCPU and 1GB per node; Scanner 1 vCPU and 2GB (2+ for HA/performance); Manager 1 vCPU and 1GB.

Scanner memory: the 2GB minimum assumes images no larger than 0.5GB. When scanning images larger than 1GB, size scanner memory as the largest image size plus 0.5GB (for example, a 1.3GB image needs 1.8GB).

The policy modes are Discover, Monitor and Protect. Any group whose name begins with 'nv', or the 'Nodes' group, can be in any of these modes; custom (user-created) groups do not have a protection mode.

In Discover mode SUSE Security learns application behaviour: it discovers containers and hosts, observes network connections, automatically builds allow-list network rules and baselines the processes in each service into process profile rules. New services start in Discover mode by default (New_Service_Policy_Mode defaults to Discover).

In Monitor mode SUSE Security detects run-time violations of the security policy and raises alerts, but does not create new rules and does not block; rules can still be added manually. Violations show as red lines in the Network Activity map and are logged in Notifications.

In Protect mode the Enforcers block (deny) network violations and detected attacks, and unauthorized processes and file access are also blocked. Blocked connections show in the Network map with a red 'x'.

Before moving to Protect, run test traffic through the application in Discover mode and review the rules; several hours is usually enough but some applications need a few days. When in doubt, switch to Monitor, check for violations and convert them to allow rules before moving to Protect.

When two communicating groups are in different modes, the effective mode for the connection is always the least restrictive of the two (for example Monitor to Protect is evaluated as Monitor, and anything involving Discover is Discover). This applies only to network rules.

Network rules are enforced in the order they appear, from top to bottom. Edits are not applied until you click Save/Deploy. If no rule matches a connection, the default action is Deny (logged as a violation in Monitor mode, blocked in Protect mode).

To allow containers to reach trusted internal services on other networks (otherwise classified as 'External'), first create a custom group in Policy → Groups with address criteria (DNS name, IP address or range), then create an Allow network rule from the source group to that group and deploy it.

SUSE Security uses X-Forwarded-For headers to identify the original (external) source IP. If this causes normal traffic through proxies or ingress to be alerted or blocked, the feature can be turned off by disabling the 'X-Forwarded-For based policy match' setting in Settings → Configuration (it is enabled by default).

SUSE Security automatically creates a 'nodes' group representing the hosts. Network connection violations of rules for the nodes group are never blocked, even in Protect mode; only process violations are blocked on nodes.
The default process/file protection changed in 5.6.1: zero-drift was the default in NeuVector 5.6.0 and older, and starting from NeuVector 5.6.1 Basic mode is the default for new deployments.

Zero-drift protection allows only processes that originate from the parent process in the original container image and does not allow file updates or new files to be installed. In Discover or Monitor mode it alerts on suspicious process or file activity; in Protect mode it blocks it. It needs no learned allow-list.

Basic process protection enforces process/file activity based on the process and file rules listed for each group, so rules must exist for protection to work. Rules can be learned in Discover mode, created in the console or REST API, or applied as a CRD. With Basic enabled and no rules in place, all activity is alerted/blocked in Monitor or Protect mode.

SUSE Security has built-in detection of common suspicious processes such as nmap and reverse shells. These are reported as suspicious process events and are NOT learned in Discover mode; if a service needs such a process, add an explicit allow process rule.

For predefined monitored files and directories and for system containers (such as Kubernetes ones), SUSE Security alerts on modifications but does not block them. Blocking is only an option for user-configured custom files/directories in non-system containers.

Registries are configured for scanning in Assets → Registries. By default only new or updated images are scanned; enable 'Rescan after CVE DB update' to rescan all images after a database update, and 'Layered Scan' to see vulnerabilities per image layer.

A registry configuration needs at least one repository filter (it cannot be blank). A filter of * or *:* scans all image tags on all registry types except the public Docker registry; regular expressions are also allowed.
Most registry scanning issues are related to registry authentication errors or the controller being unable to access the registry from the cluster.

Run-time scanning of containers, nodes and the platform is enabled with Auto-Scan in the Vulnerabilities tab of Assets → Nodes or Containers. With Auto-Scan on, newly started assets are scanned and all running assets are rescanned after a CVE database update.
The updater cron job sample (neuvector-updater.yaml, schedule "0 0 * * *") is created with kubectl create; it is normally already deployed by the sample deployments.

Admission Control is disabled by default. Enable it in the console under Policy → Admission Control; once enabled, a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration named neuvector-validating-admission-webhook is created automatically.
After enabling Admission Control, verify the automatically created webhook resource with kubectl get ValidatingWebhookConfiguration neuvector-validating-admission-webhook.
Admission control has two modes: Monitor, where a denied decision only logs an alert and the resource is still created, and Protect, an inline mode where denied resources are not created.

Admission control rules are Allow or Deny rules; Allow rules are evaluated first to define exceptions to Deny rules. Matching order is default allow rules, federated allow, federated deny, CRD allow, CRD deny, user-defined allow, user-defined deny; if nothing matches, the request is allowed.

If an admission criterion requires an image scan but the image has not been scanned, that part of the rule is ignored. To prevent unscanned images from bypassing scan-based rules, use the 'Image scanned' criterion.

A kube-apiserver log entry 'Failed calling webhook, failing open ... no such host' for neuvector-svc-admission-webhook means the API server cannot resolve the admission webhook service name. A 'x509: certificate is valid for ...' error means the caBundle certificate is wrong, and 'service ... not found' means the webhook service is missing.
When troubleshooting admission control, check the neuvector-binding-admission clusterrole; its verbs must include get, list, watch, create, update and delete, otherwise the Test button fails.

SUSE Security automatically runs CIS benchmarks for Kubernetes, Docker, Red Hat OpenShift (draft 'Inspired by CIS') and Google GKE. Compliance profile templates exist for PCI, GDPR, HIPAA, NIST (SP 800-190), PCIv4 and DISA STIG, and reports are generated in Security Risks → Compliance.

When deployed from Rancher (Rancher Extensions or Apps & Marketplace), SUSE Security is installed with the Helm chart into the cattle-neuvector-system namespace. In the chart values, set the container run-time to match the cluster: docker for RKE, containerd for RKE2, or the K3s value for K3s.

The default SUSE Security console login is admin / admin, and you are prompted to change it on first login. For Rancher deployments it is recommended to log in directly to the console as admin to set a strong password, or to supply a ConfigMap (as a secret) at deployment to set the default admin password.
The SUSE Security Helm guide for Rancher installs starts by adding the Rancher charts repository and updating it.
Before installing the main chart, install the neuvector-crd chart from rancher-charts into the cattle-neuvector-system namespace.
If the cluster has Pod Security Admission (PSA) enabled, label the cattle-neuvector-system namespace to allow privileged containers.

Install the main SUSE Security chart from rancher-charts with a values.yaml that sets global.cattle.url to the Rancher URL, controller.federation.managedsvc.type to NodePort and global.cattle.systemDefaultRegistry to the Prime registry URL.
command: helm install neuvector --namespace cattle-neuvector-system --create-namespace rancher-charts/neuvector --version={chart-version} -f values.yaml

fact: After a Helm install from rancher-charts, find the NodePort for the SUSE Security UI from the neuvector-service-webui service; the console listens on port 8443.

The documented air-gapped install uses three tools: Helm, Skopeo and ZStandard (zstd). The chart is pulled from the neuvector Helm repository, images are listed from the rendered chart and copied with skopeo into tar archives, everything is compressed with tar and zstd, moved inside, and the images are loaded into the internal registry with skopeo.

For an air-gapped install, after adding the neuvector Helm repo (helm repo add neuvector https://neuvector.github.io/neuvector-helm/) and updating it, download the chart into a local directory with helm pull neuvector/core -d neuvector.
To see orchestration activity for SUSE Security pods (creation timestamps, status, deployments, DaemonSets), inspect Kubernetes events in the neuvector namespace.

Debug mode for all controllers can be turned on from the SUSE Security CLI (run inside the manager pod with 'cli' and 'login'). Debug logging greatly increases log size, so turn it off after collecting logs.

The support log, which contains system configuration, containers, policies, notifications and SUSE Security container details for Support, is downloaded from Settings → Configuration by selecting Collect Log.

To keep controllers available during node maintenance or autoscaling, create a PodDisruptionBudget (the sample nv_pdb.yaml uses minAvailable: 2 with selector app: neuvector-controller-pod) and apply it with kubectl create -f nv_pdb.yaml.

Persistent configuration backup uses a volume mounted at /var/neuvector in the controller pod, which requires a ReadWriteMany (RWX) PersistentVolume (1Gi or more). Without a persistent volume, configuration and policy are not stored persistently, so back up the configuration from Settings → Configuration or run 3 or 5 controllers.

When upgrading controllers to 5.6.0 or later from a version that does not support critical-level severity (for example 5.5.3), existing scanner pods must be restarted or redeployed, because older scanners cache the controller's initial capability response.

SUSE Security supports security policy as code through CRDs: NvSecurityRule (namespace-scoped), NvClusterSecurityRule (cluster-scoped), NvAdmissionControlSecurityRule and NvGroupDefinition. A policy mode set in an imported CRD cannot be changed from the console; change it in the CRD.
To update CRD-defined SUSE Security rules, edit the yaml file and apply it with kubectl apply.

SUSE Security can be configured automatically with a Kubernetes ConfigMap named neuvector-init (sample initcfg.yaml) created with kubectl create. It is read only at initial startup or after a complete cluster restart unless always_reload: true is set.

On SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP7, register the system with SUSE Customer Center from the command line with SUSEConnect, passing the registration code and the e-mail address of the SUSE account. This also registers the Basesystem and Server Applications modules and adds their repositories.
To register SLES against a local registration server (for example RMT) instead of SUSE Customer Center, add the --url option with the server URL to the SUSEConnect registration command.
On a registered SLES 15 SP7 system, list the available modules and extensions, with their activation commands and product identifiers, using SUSEConnect --list-extensions.

Activate a module on SLES with SUSEConnect -p followed by the product identifier in the form name/version/architecture, for example sle-module-containers/15.7/x86_64 for the Containers Module on SLES 15 SP7.

SLES extensions such as High Availability, Workstation Extension and Live Patching need their own additional registration code, passed with -r when activating them, for example SUSEConnect -p sle-ha/15.7/x86_64 -r ADDITIONAL REGCODE. Modules such as Containers or Development Tools need no extra code.

SUSEConnect only registers or deregisters modules and extensions and enables or disables their repositories; it does not install or remove packages. After removing a module with SUSEConnect, its packages remain installed but get no more updates; list them with zypper packages --orphaned.
Never delete the Basesystem Module from a SLES system, and do not delete the Server Applications Module either. These are the default modules registered with SLES.

To completely deregister a SLES system, including all modules and extensions, run SUSEConnect -d. This removes the system's entry on the registration server and removes the repositories for the product, modules and extensions.

Since SUSEConnect 0.3.33, the suseconnect-keepalive.timer runs SUSEConnect --keep-alive once a day to report the system's last-seen time and hardware information to the registration server. It is enabled automatically and can be disabled with systemctl.

SLES 15 offers an NVIDIA Compute Module containing the NVIDIA CUDA drivers, activated with SUSEConnect -p sle-module-NVIDIA-compute/15/x86_64 (its version is 15, not 15.7). The software is provided by NVIDIA under the CUDA EULA and is not supported by SUSE; because its GPG key is unknown, add --gpg-auto-import-keys when activating.

On SLES, zypper patch installs all officially released patches that apply to the system (except optional and feature patches). SUSE documentation calls patching the most reliable way to install new versions of installed packages, and it warns before installing a patch that needs a reboot.
To list the patches that apply to a SLES system but are not yet installed, use zypper list-patches; zypper patches lists all patches regardless of whether they are installed or apply.
To install only the patches for a specific CVE on SLES, use zypper patch --cve=NUMBER, for example zypper patch --cve=CVE-2010-2713; --bugzilla=NUMBER does the same for a Bugzilla issue.

zypper patch installs official patches and reports a conflict if a package is considered vulnerable, while zypper update updates all installed packages to newer available versions and silently skips problematic ones such as locked packages. Use zypper update when a repository provides new packages but no patches.

After patching or updating SLES, run zypper ps to list running processes that still use files deleted by the update; when a process belongs to a known service, the service name is shown so it can be restarted.
