If zypper cannot find a package you know exists in a configured repository, first run zypper refresh; if that does not help, run zypper refresh -fdb, which forces a complete refresh and rebuild of the database, including a forced download of raw metadata.

On SLES the official update repository is only available after the installation has been registered, so an unregistered system gets no official patches from zypper patch; register it with SUSEConnect or YaST first.

SUSE Linux Micro uses a read-only root file system, so you cannot change it directly with zypper. Instead, transactional-update applies changes into a new snapshot, which becomes active only after you reboot into it.

On SUSE Linux Micro, install a package with transactional-update pkg install package_name; it accepts the same options as zypper install, can install patterns with -t pattern, and the package is available after a reboot.

On SUSE Linux Micro, transactional-update patch checks for available patches and installs them into a new snapshot (non-interactive by default); running transactional-update without any arguments also updates the system. Reboot to activate the result.

Register SUSE Linux Micro from the command line with transactional-update register -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS (as root); add --url to use a local registration server. The register command also supports --list-extensions, -p, -d and -s/--status.

By default each transactional-update run creates a new snapshot from the current root file system, so running it twice without rebooting gives two independent snapshots and the second does not contain the first change. To combine changes before a reboot, use --continue, transactional-update run, or transactional-update shell.

transactional-update shell opens a read-write shell in a new snapshot, where you can run zypper and edit files on the read-only root; all changes go into one snapshot, and you exit and reboot to apply them. You cannot start or stop services or modify /var inside it.

To roll back SUSE Linux Micro from a running system, find the snapshot number with snapper list, set it as default with transactional-update rollback snapshot_number (or rollback last for the last working snapshot), then reboot.

Automatic updates on SUSE Linux Micro are enabled by default through transactional-update.timer, which runs once a day, applies all updates and informs rebootmgrd that the machine should reboot. Disable them with systemctl --now disable transactional-update.timer.

Inside a transactional-update environment, /var is not part of the snapshot and is not accessible, and the working directory is set to / rather than the directory you ran the command from; some directories, such as /root, are not in the snapshot but are accessible.

Cockpit is included in the default type of SUSE Linux Micro pre-built images but not in the base type; to install it, run transactional-update pkg install -t pattern cockpit as root and reboot into the new snapshot.

To make a machine a primary Cockpit server, enable the socket with systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket; systemd then starts cockpit-ws listening on port 9090, and the web interface is at https://IP_ADDRESS_OF_MACHINE:9090.
If firewalld is enabled, open Cockpit with firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=cockpit and then reload the firewall with firewall-cmd --reload.

On new SUSE Linux Micro installations, Cockpit does not allow root to log in with a password by default. Create an unprivileged user and switch to administrative access in Cockpit, or (discouraged) remove root from /etc/cockpit/disallowed-users. SUSE recommends adding 2FA.

On SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0, Cockpit can be installed during installation with Agama or later on the running system with zypper in -t pattern cockpit; check whether it is installed with zypper se -i cockpit.

Choose SUSE Linux BCI-Base (registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base) when you need flexibility: it includes Zypper and the free SLE_BCI repository so you can install packages during the build, but it is the largest general-purpose BCI (about 135 MB for 15.7), so it is not always the best deployment image.

SUSE Linux BCI-Minimal is a stripped-down BCI-Base without Zypper but with the RPM package manager. RPM can install packages but has no repository support or automatic dependency resolution, so the image is intended for deployment containers.

SUSE Linux BCI-Micro is like BCI-Minimal but without the RPM package manager. It is meant for deploying static binaries built externally or in multi-stage builds, and SUSE recommends it only when the artifact bundles all its dependencies and needs no external runtime such as Python or Ruby.

SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox provides only basic tools, implemented by the BusyBox project. It is the smallest glibc-based general-purpose BCI (about 12 MB for 15.7) and contains no GPLv3-licensed software. Its tools differ from GNU Coreutils, so scripts may need changes, and it has no bash.

SUSE Linux BCIs do not require a subscription to run or distribute, and a permissive EULA allows redistributing custom images built on them. Each SLES service pack has a free SLE_BCI repository, a subset of the SLE repository with over 4000 packages, and SUSE can provide support for BCIs through SUSE subscription plans.

Pin SUSE Linux BCIs to an explicit version tag such as registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 instead of :latest. The BCI family's :latest tag is migrating image by image from SLES 15 to SUSE Linux 16 (bci-nano first), and SLES 15 SP7 BCIs are maintained until the end of general support for SP7 (31 July 2031).

The support level of a SUSE Linux BCI is exposed as the com.suse.supportlevel label (for example l3 = full support, techpreview = unsupported proof of concept) and can be read without pulling the image using skopeo and jq.

Development Stack SUSE Linux BCIs are built on BCI-Base and include Zypper, the SLE_BCI repository and language tooling. Examples are python (python3 plus pip3), node (nodejs plus npm), openjdk, openjdk-devel, ruby, rust, golang, gcc, dotnet-runtime, dotnet-aspnet, dotnet-sdk, php, php-apache and php-fpm. They follow the language stack's support lifecycle, not the SLES one.

Long Term Service Pack Support (LTSS) container images on registry.suse.com require a valid LTSS subscription and a registry login. You can log in with a host's SCC credentials, with a registration code using the literal user name regcode, or with organization mirroring credentials.

To use SUSE Application Collection Helm charts, log Helm in to the Distribution Platform at dp.apps.rancher.io. Use your username with an access token (user account) or a service account's username with its secret.

To run SUSE Application Collection images in Kubernetes, create a docker-registry pull secret for dp.apps.rancher.io (conventionally named application-collection) with your username or service-account username and the access token or service-account secret.

SUSE Application Collection charts are installed from oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/<name>. Every chart supports the standardized global.imagePullSecrets option, which names the pull secret; add --version to choose a chart version and use helm show values to see the options.

SUSE Application Collection supports user accounts (username plus access token) and service accounts (username plus secret). A user account inherits the subscriptions of all the user's organizations, while a service account belongs to one organization, gets only that organization's subscriptions, has less restrictive rate limits, is recommended for machine-to-machine use, and can only be created by organization admins.

An image pull secret passed with global.imagePullSecrets must already exist in the namespace where the Application Collection chart is deployed. To pull from a private mirror, combine global.imageRegistry with global.imagePullSecrets.

Installing SUSE AI Library applications requires the SUSE AI entitlement, which is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime. The entitlement check is done at https://apps.rancher.io/; when it succeeds, you can pull and deploy the SUSE AI Helm charts and container images from SUSE Application Collection.

For SUSE AI 1.0 cluster nodes, SUSE recommends SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP6 as a traditional non-transactional OS or SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 as an immutable transactional OS, with SUSE Rancher Prime: RKE2 as the Kubernetes distribution. NVIDIA GPU drivers are installed on the GPU nodes.
For production SUSE AI deployments, SUSE strongly recommends deploying Rancher, SUSE Observability and the AI Library workloads to separate Kubernetes clusters.

SUSE AI Library charts and images come from both SUSE Application Collection and SUSE Registry. In addition to the application-collection secret, create a SUSE Registry pull secret (suse-ai-registry) whose username is the literal regcode and whose password is the SCC registration code of the SUSE AI subscription.

To steer SUSE AI workloads to GPU nodes, label the GPU nodes (the guide uses accelerator=nvidia-gpu) and set a matching nodeSelector in the chart's values; check labels with kubectl get nodes --show-labels.

After the NVIDIA GPU Operator is configured, SUSE AI applications get GPUs by requesting the nvidia.com/gpu resource in requests and limits in values.yaml. GPU passthrough must also be enabled in the Helm chart; otherwise the container may still run but uses only the CPU.

When the NVIDIA GPU Operator runs with host-installed drivers (driver.enabled false), the node label nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver should read pre-installed. If it reads true, the drivers were not correctly installed, possibly because the node was not rebooted after installing the packages. Note that the operator restarts containerd, which restarts RKE2.

To install NVIDIA GPU drivers on SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 for SUSE AI, open a transactional-update shell, add the NVIDIA repository and install the open driver packages with zypper inside it, exit, reboot into the new snapshot, and verify with nvidia-smi. For modern GPUs, the G06 driver generation is the most common choice.

SUSE AI Library applications in the SUSE AI 1.0 guide include cert-manager, OpenSearch or Milvus (vector database for Open WebUI), Ollama, Open WebUI, vLLM, mcpo, PyTorch, Qdrant, LiteLLM, MLflow and Kubeflow. cert-manager is no longer part of the Open WebUI chart and must be installed separately first, and Open WebUI installs Ollama by default.

In SUSE AI, Ollama is installed from SUSE Application Collection with helm upgrade --install from oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama into the SUSE AI namespace, using an override values file; inspect its options with helm show values oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama.
